PCI.BIO: Keith Joseph is a Clinical Assistant Professor of clinical medicine and pathophysiology in the Physician Assistant department at UTRGV, Edinburg since 2017. He received a B.S. in Biology from UT at San Antonio in 2008, and a Master of Public Health from the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (UTHealth) School of Public Health in 2016. He received his MD from the UT School of Medicine at San Antonio in 2016.

PCI_RESEARCH_INTERESTS.DESC: His research interest during his undergraduate and graduate studies was on HIV receptor research. His work focused primarily on defining host factors that influence susceptibility to HIV and AIDS.

PASTHIST.TITLE: Clinical Trial Coordinator
PASTHIST.DESC:
Assist the Principle Investigator as he fulfills his role of conduct and oversight of clinical trials. I am also
responsible for recruiting, screening, monitoring vital signs, and observing reactions and symptoms of
study participants. Additionally, I oversee the consent process, ensuring that all questions are
answered satisfactorily and that study protocol requirements are adhered to, thus ensuring the safety
of our patients and robust efficacy of our trials.

PASTHIST.TITLE: Research Associate
PASTHIST.DESC:
Work on projects related to defining host factors that influence susceptibility to HIV and AIDS.Use state
of the art molecular biology and genotyping techniques such as real-time PCR, and PCR/RFLP assays to
isolate genes related to host defense and immunity. Employ critical thinking in the design of projects
and their execution. Submitted an abstract for participation in the Annual Frontiers of Translational
Science Research Day at UTHSCSA. My work showed that HLA-B*51 is associated with enhanced cellmediated
immune responses and delayed disease progression to AIDS, serving as evidence for
adaptation to HLA-B*51 at the population level. Research projects focused on elucidating the role of
HLA in HIV susceptibility and disease progression.

PASTHIST.TITLE: Quality Assurance Analyst
PASTHIST.DESC:
Audited FDA regulated drug and device phase I, II and III studies. Represented the company at FDA
Inspections. My contribution analyzing clinical data and identifying protocol deviations helped the
company pass several FDA audits. This research experience reinforced in me the value of teamwork,
excellent history taking, and detailed patient examination.

PRESENT.NAME: UTHSCSA 11th Annual Department of Medicine Research Day
PRESENT.TITLE: The genetic background conferred by variations in CCL3L1-CCR5
PRESENT.ABSTRACT:
C-X-C motif receptor 4 (CXCR4) is a key HIV-1 coreceptor. Unlike for the other major HIV-1 coreceptor, CC chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5), few studies have examined the impact of single nucleotide
polymorphisms (SNPs) in CXCR4 on HIV-1/AIDS susceptibility. Our objective was to determine the effect of CXCR4 SNPs on the influence of  HIV-1 acquisition and disease progression.

PRESENT.NAME: UT SOM at San Antonio 2nd Annual Frontiers of Translational Science Research Day
PRESENT.TITLE: HLA-B*51 associates with enhanced cell-mediated immune responses and delayed progression to AIDS
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: HLA class I molecules determine the repertoire of viral peptides that are presented by antigen presenting cells, in turn, shaping the immune response to HIV. HLA-B*51 associates strongly with increased susceptibility to Behcet’s Disease, but its influence on cell-mediated immunity (CMI) or HIV-1 disease progression has not been fully explored.  To address this, we evaluated first, 205 healthy adults from Australia in whom CMI was assessed by delayed type hypersensitivity (DTH) skin test reactivity to the neoantigen KLH and second, 178 HIV-1 perinatally infected children from Ukraine. Stepwise multiple regression models retained the HLA-B*51 allele (P=<0.001) as the strongest association for increased DTH responses (OR= 2.73; P=0.022).

PRESENT.NAME: UTHSCSA San Antonio Research Day 2010
PRESENT.TITLE: Interaction of Genetic Variations in IL-10 and CCR5 in Demented Adult Patients
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: As our population grows older dementia, and particularly Alzheimer’s disease (AD), is becoming a more serious problem in our society. It is imperative that we quickly find a solution. Based on their known functions, CCR5, a chemokine receptor mostly known for its role in HIV infection, and IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine, may play a role in AD pathogenesis. We used a genetic association approach to evaluate whether CCR5 and IL-10 may have additive effects on risk of AD development.

PRESENT.ABSTRACT: A honors thesis presentation of my research on the Influence of CXCR4 Polymorphisms on HIV-1/AIDS Susceptibility
